question: What let the 2026-11-11 incident happen, and how do proven systems prevent each part of it?
found: Measured: after the reboot the agent replayed the afternoon's jobs from the oldest (102 started, 40 ok, 62 failed - mostly guards refusing), fifty at a time after a reconnect, on shared clones; it had inferred 'pending' from a missing result. Before that it stalled at 22:29 CET with nothing logged until the reboot. No alert could reach the author - every channel went through the agent. Harm: none - four replayed pull requests, all the legitimate tad 0.4.0 pin bump; no direct pushes, tags, releases or phone actions; tools and clones restored. The root: a job is a script with no record of its life. Proven answers: durable execution's event history and heartbeats (Temporal), leases with fencing tokens (Kleppmann; Patterns of Distributed Systems), a dead man's switch watched from elsewhere (Healthchecks), crash-only recovery (Candea and Fox), run-once jobs with deadlines (Kubernetes), idempotency keys (Stripe), a working tree per job (git worktree). Replayed 2026-11-12: the old agent's real log of 2026-11-11, read line by line through oco-agent's rules (oco-agent/replay): of the 357 jobs the old agent started over six runs, oco-agent would have started 255 and refused exactly 102, each because it had already finished - the first at 23:16:24, the moment the replay began. The journal it kept (764 rows of tad data) checks out and answers SQL. 2026-11-12, from the whole system's log: the machine did not sleep and its network stayed up through the stall; a USB device was disconnected at 22:25:28 with nothing after it going wrong, so the phone looks innocent. The stall was inside lab-agent's daemon. Its GitHub client is built with no limit on how long a request may take (src/github.rs: ureq::AgentBuilder::new().build()), so one connection that hangs holds the polling loop for ever - which fits every fact, though nobody watched it hang. oco-agent's client limits every request to 20 s. The desktop is set to suspend after an hour without input, and lab-agent keeps it awake only while a job runs. 2026-11-12, proven: the replays come from lab-agent's reading of what is done. already_handled lists its results folder through GitHub's contents API, which returns at most 1,000 entries and says nothing of the rest: the folder held 1,135; the first replayed job of the second replay (1794436981-after-reconnect) had its result, but was not among the 1,000 listed. Every job past the thousandth looked unfinished. Both replays - 102 jobs on 2026-11-11 and 25 after the boot on 2026-11-12 - share this one cause. The 2026-11-12 replay changed no repository (no commits since the boot) but put tad 0.4.0 back on the lab (restored to 0.5.0). 2026-11-12, later - the stall is proven too, and it has the same cause as the replays. lab-agent sees new jobs through the same contents listing of its jobs folder, cut silently at 1,000 entries. The folder holds a placeholder, .keep, which sorts before every job; when lab-agent started its last job before the stall (22:29:23), the folder held 999 jobs - with .keep, exactly 1,000. Every job submitted after that lay past the end of the listing: the agent was alive, polling, and blind. The earlier note here that a request with no time limit was the probable cause was wrong as the main cause; time limits are added anyway, since a hang should never be silent either. One cause - a listing that stops without a word - made the stall, the replay of 102 jobs, and the replay of 25 after the boot.

question: What does everything we run cost from GitHub's hourly budget?
found: Measured 2026-11-12: 759 of 5,000 used in an hour of heavy work. The budget is one for the whole account: lab-agent's daemon, the client's submits and waits, land waiting on CI, the pin updater, the probes and oco-agent all draw on it. lab-agent's daemon, wait and board already ask conditionally (ETag), so idle polling every 5 s is free; oco-agent's first GitHub adapter did not, and would have spent about 30 a minute listening (about 480 an hour at its default pace). With conditional listings its cost while nothing changes is nothing but its first two answers: a minute of listening every 4 s counted 2, against 5 for a baseline minute in which only the measuring job's own log streaming ran - oco-agent's share is lost in that noise. A folder that does not exist answers 404 every time, charged and with no fingerprint, so the asked-work folder keeps a README and a missing listing is not asked again for two minutes. Content creation (commits through the API, pull requests) has its own lower limits, worth minding in rollouts.

question: What should the redesigned lab-agent be called?
found: The author proposed oco-agent (2026-11-12): it is built on ocoeco by design. Prior art names this role - a long-running program on a machine that takes jobs and runs them - an agent (Jenkins, Buildkite, TeamCity) or a runner (GitHub, GitLab). 'agent' also means an AI agent; the design already separates them: the AI driving the lab is the driver, the program is the machine's hands and voice. 'lab' said where it runs, not what it belongs to; 'oco-' says its family and the direction of dependency (built on ocoeco, which knows nothing of it).

question: How should waiting be counted, and how can work go on while a long job runs?
found: Waiting is one of the seven wastes of the Toyota Production System; Kanban measures flow efficiency - time worked over total time - so manual work (effort) and waiting (idle time) are two halves of one measure. Little's law: shorter waits or more work in flight raise throughput. Make and CI run independent jobs side by side and serialise only those sharing a resource. So: lab-agent records every wait itself, with what is waited on and for which project; and jobs declare the resources they hold, so those that do not conflict run in parallel.
